title: The Automation Mandate
headline: Built reporting and SOP systems that removed 12+ hours of weekly manual work.
summary: Three departments were losing time to the same manual reporting routine every week. The fix was less about software and more about giving the process real rules.
problem: Finance, sales, and ops were all touching the same data, reformatting the same spreadsheets, handing off the same half-finished files. It worked, technically — but it ate too much time and broke whenever someone forgot a step.
intervention: I mapped out the reporting path, rebuilt the recurring workbook logic in Excel, and wrote SOPs so the same steps happen every cycle. The point wasn't the spreadsheet — it was making the process run the same way every week without anyone having to reinvent it.
outcome: About 12 hours of manual work came off the weekly rhythm. But the bigger win was that people stopped dreading the process. Handoffs stopped breaking, and the whole thing could survive someone being out sick.
evidenceBullets: Built automated reports in Excel that took roughly 12 hours of manual work out of the weekly cycle.
Wrote shared SOPs across finance, sales, and operations so the process stopped depending on one person's memory.
Moved the work from 'someone needs to remember this' to 'this just runs now'.

narrative.title: Case Context
narrative.body: The problem wasn't effort — it was structure. People were remembering the right sequence from last week and touching the same information too many times. Every Monday was a fresh scramble.

narrative.title: What I Built
narrative.body: I treated the workflow like a system, not just a spreadsheet. Combined workbook automation with clearer rules for who owns what and documented steps that made the cycle easy to execute and easy to hand off.

narrative.title: Why It Mattered
narrative.body: The gain wasn't only time. People had a cleaner rhythm, fewer avoidable delays, and a process that could run consistently week after week without depending on any single person.

impact.label: hours saved weekly
impact.note: Manual reporting effort removed from the recurring cycle.

impact.label: functions aligned
impact.note: Finance, sales, and operations worked from one clearer structure.

impact.label: shared operating rhythm
impact.note: Automation and SOPs combined into a repeatable weekly flow.

board.preview: A reporting cycle that was eating 12 hours of manual work every week got rebuilt into something that runs itself.

title: KPI-Based Governance
headline: Led a 34-member organization through KPI governance, structured programs, and cleaner execution.
summary: A 34-member student council across 10 divisions needed a better way to see what was working and what wasn't. I introduced KPIs and weekly check-ins to give leadership and execution a cleaner cadence.
problem: Once you hit 10 divisions and 34 people, group chats and good intentions don't cut it anymore. The council needed real visibility into which programs were progressing and which were stalling.
intervention: I led the organization with KPIs, weekly reviews, clearer division expectations, and a stronger planning approach for school-wide programs. Nothing fancy — just structure where there wasn't any.
outcome: We could finally see what was moving and what was stuck. Programs ran more steadily, outreach reached 12 feeder schools, and the council started operating like an institution instead of a friend group.
evidenceBullets: Ran a 34-person council across 10 divisions with KPIs and weekly check-ins.
Built institutional programs that the school itself ended up adopting.
Led outreach campaigns that reached 12 feeder schools.

narrative.title: Case Context
narrative.body: Once a student org goes multi-division, running on informal leadership doesn't work anymore. Without structure, momentum gets uneven and nobody's sure who's actually accountable.

narrative.title: What I Changed
narrative.body: I brought in a governance model with measurable expectations, recurring checkpoints, and better alignment between what each division was doing and what the council needed overall.

narrative.title: Why It Mattered
narrative.body: The council grew up. It was easier to see what was actually moving, what was blocked, and where leadership energy needed to go next.

impact.label: members led
impact.note: Leadership scope across the full organization.

impact.label: divisions coordinated
impact.note: Governance structure applied across the council.

impact.label: feeder schools reached
impact.note: Scale of one major outward-facing campaign effort.

board.preview: A 34-person council needed to stop running on vibes. KPIs and weekly rhythms gave it real accountability.

title: Large-Scale Event Ops
headline: Kept live event execution stable across 1,000+ attendee environments and high-pressure transitions.
summary: Big public events compress time, pressure, and risk into one live window. My job was keeping the backstage tight enough that the audience never noticed the work.
problem: When you have 1,000+ people watching, a sloppy transition doesn't just feel bad — it's visible to everyone. Live programs need precise timing, shared coordination, and zero room for improvisation.
intervention: I coordinated stage and backstage execution, supported transition planning, and kept the pacing tight enough that tech crews, speakers, performers, and the audience stayed in sync.
outcome: Events ran with cleaner transitions, more predictable stage flow, and solid control during the moments where timing really mattered.
evidenceBullets: Ran backstage coordination for events with 1,000+ people.
MC'd Youth Mass 2025 for 500+ participants — kept pacing tight from start to finish.
Cut down transition friction by giving every crew a clear, documented sequence.

narrative.title: Case Context
narrative.body: When a transition is even slightly unclear, the whole room sees it. The challenge isn't creating wow moments — it's making sure the boring parts (cues, pacing, handoffs) don't turn into visible failures.

narrative.title: How I Operated
narrative.body: I sat right between planning and execution. My job was turning the show flow into something the tech crew and on-stage participants could follow without hesitating. That meant tighter transition plans and constant communication.

narrative.title: Why It Mattered
narrative.body: When pacing holds, the event feels intentional. When it breaks, everyone notices. Consistency protects the audience experience — that's the whole point.

impact.label: audience scale handled
impact.note: Large live-event environments with visible execution pressure.

impact.label: participants led as MC
impact.note: Youth Mass 2025 served as a clear proof point for live communication under pressure.

impact.label: active event period
impact.note: Sustained involvement across multiple execution environments.

board.preview: 1,000+ people watching, and the only thing visible is what fails. This file covers the backstage systems that kept things clean.

title: Vertical Rescue Ops
headline: Supported equipment readiness, technical training, and operational discipline over 4+ active years.
summary: Readiness work doesn't get filmed. But when things go wrong in the field, it's the only thing that matters. Equipment, people, and process all have to be solid before the situation demands it.
problem: In technical rescue, you can't improvise once things get serious. Equipment has to be checked, training has to be consistent, and everyone needs to know their role before anyone is actually in danger.
intervention: I took care of equipment maintenance, supported technical climbing sessions, and helped keep the training standard high. Not glamorous — just the kind of work that has to be right every time.
outcome: Equipment stayed ready. Training sessions ran more smoothly. And the people coming into the program had a better foundation before they ever hit a real situation.
evidenceBullets: Kept equipment inspection-ready through regular maintenance.
Supported climbing and belay sessions as part of the training team.
Helped build a culture where preparation isn't optional — it's the baseline.

narrative.title: Case Context
narrative.body: In technical rescue, the challenge isn't dramatic moments. It's making sure the basics are solid long before the stakes get real. Equipment checks, training reps, role clarity — none of it can be improvised.

narrative.title: What the Work Required
narrative.body: I took care of equipment, supported training sessions, and kept things reliable. That meant showing up, paying attention to repeatable standards, and making the environment safer and more useful for everyone.

narrative.title: Why It Mattered
narrative.body: Confidence in the field comes from preparation. When readiness work is done right, it reduces uncertainty, makes training better, and keeps high-risk situations grounded in discipline instead of guesswork.

impact.label: years active
impact.note: Sustained involvement in readiness and training work.

impact.label: equipment discipline
impact.note: Inspection and maintenance practices remained part of the operating standard.

impact.label: training support role
impact.note: Hands-on contribution in practical climbing and belay environments.

board.preview: The quieter side of high-risk work: inspection routines, training support, and the discipline that keeps things dependable when it counts.
